query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled pre‐oxidation surface treatment (i.e., a brief anneal at ~800 °C under a controlled oxygen partial pressure) applied to cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will induce the formation of a thin, dense, and adherent protective oxide layer (predominantly HfO2 with possible contributions from Nb/Ta oxides) that retards oxygen ingress during subsequent high‐temperature air exposure, thus preventing pesting without compromising the alloy’s inherent room‐ and high‐temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, exhibiting an as-cast microstructure.
generation.intervention: A single-step, pre-oxidation thermal treatment (anneal) at approximately 800 °C for a short duration (e.g., ~1 hour) under a controlled oxygen partial pressure (e.g., atmosphere with moderated oxygen content) to form a pre-passivating surface oxide.
generation.conditions: Treatment: ~800 °C for ~1 hour in a controlled oxygen environment; Testing: subsequent exposure in air at 800–1000 °C for up to 5 hours under tensile loading at strain rates between 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a thin, dense, and adherent oxide layer primarily composed of HfO2 (with possible Nb/Ta oxide contributions) that serves as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
generation.mechanism: The pre-formed protective oxide minimizes further oxygen ingress during high-temperature exposure by acting as a diffusion barrier, thereby mitigating the pesting (rapid oxidation) phenomenon while leaving the bulk microstructure and mechanical properties intact.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated material, the pre-oxidized alloy is expected to exhibit significantly improved oxygen resistance (reduced oxide scale growth and pesting) during extended high-temperature air exposures (800–1000 °C, up to 5 hours) without a measurable degradation in room-temperature ductility (8–16%) or high-temperature yield strength.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which suffers from inadequate oxygen resistance (pesting) despite favorable mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: Temperature: 800–1000 °C; Atmosphere: Air (with control treatment in a moderate oxygen environment); Exposure Time: Up to 5 hours; Loading: Tensile tests at strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1.
generation.uncertainty: The precise composition, thickness, and long-term adhesion of the protective oxide under cyclic or prolonged service conditions remain uncertain. Additionally, the optimum controlled oxygen partial pressure and treatment time to balance oxide formation with bulk property preservation require further refinement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples: one group receives the controlled pre-oxidation treatment (anneal at ~800 °C for ~1 hour in a moderated oxygen environment), while the other is left untreated. Subject both groups to an extended air exposure test at 800–1000 °C for 5 hours under representative tensile loading conditions (strain rates 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1). Post-exposure, characterize the surface for oxide scale thickness, continuity, and phase composition using methods such as XRD, SEM, and TEM, and re-assess mechanical properties (room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength).
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and uniformity (using SEM/TEM)
Phase composition of the oxide layer (using XRD)
Retention of mechanical properties (tensile ductility and yield strength evaluations)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxide scale growth or retardation of oxygen ingress compared to the untreated samples, or if the beneficial mechanical properties (ductility or yield strength) are degraded beyond acceptable limits post-treatment, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

Investigations of mechanical properties and microstructure of different MEAs derived from the HfNbTaTiZr alloy system has been performed. It has been shown that ductility is significantly reduced by simultaneous presence of Ta and Zr in the alloy, which leads to reduction of the BCC1 phase content. These elements segregate during solidifying. Because of the miscibility gap in the Ta-Zr equilibrium phase diagram two BCC phases are found after cooling to room temperature. Clear correlation between the BCC1 phase content and the total elongation to failure of the alloy was found. Precipitation of Ta rich precipitates on grain boundaries reduces the elongation to almost zero values. No correlation was found between the tensile mechanical properties and microstructure related parameters in investigated set of alloys. The 5 element HEA alloy exhibits the best combination of strength and elongation. 4 and 3 element MEAs have lower strength to various extent. Some of them are ductile (NbTaTiZr, NbTaTi, NbTiZr) but some of them are brittle (TaTiZr, Nb1.5TaTiZr0.5, Nb0.5TaTiZr1.5) depending on microstructure. decision.trend: Early work in refractory and high‐entropy systems addressed oxidation issues first by trying compositional adjustments – for example, the non‐equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy work showed that modest changes can arrest pesting under high‐temperature air exposure. Later, studies in related systems (for example, the amorphous AlCrTiZrMo HEA film work) demonstrated that processing routes which induce the in‐situ formation of a dense, adherent oxide scale (such as a ZrTiO4 composite layer) are effective at retarding oxygen ingress. In these cases, a controlled thermal treatment promoted a beneficial surface oxide without adversely altering the favorable bulk mechanical properties. Nonetheless, no similar surface‐engineering intervention has been demonstrated for the equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr, leaving its oxidation (pesting) problem unresolved.
decision.unsolved: The equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr remains vulnerable to rapid, deleterious oxidation (pesting) at temperatures around 800–1000 °C. Although related non‐equiatomic alloy systems and films have shown that a pre‐formed protective oxide can improve high‐temperature oxygen resistance, there is still no single, proven intervention for this composition that preserves its established room‐ and high‐temperature mechanical performance.
decision.lever: Apply a controlled, pre‐oxidation surface treatment (for example, a brief anneal at about 800 °C in a controlled oxygen partial pressure environment) to induce the formation of a thin, dense, and adherent protective oxide scale (predominantly HfO2 possibly mixed with minor Nb/Ta oxides) on the as-cast alloy surfaces.
decision.why: This approach logically extends the trend from related studies where thermal treatments enable the in-situ formation of self-passivating oxide layers that arrest oxygen ingress without altering the bulk composition or mechanical properties. It directly targets the oxygen resistance issue through surface modification – a single intervention that complies with the design constraints – as supported by evidence from the earlier oxidation‐protection work on a related non‐equiatomic system and the HER film study.
